To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

crossing of two transgenic lines of mice, one expressing mutant human APP and the other mutant human tau, results in accelerated amyloid deposition, increased neurofibrillary tangle formation, and enhanced neuronal loss in brain regions that are selectively vulnerable in Alzheimer's disease.

1) the co-expression of mutant human amyloid precursor protein (APP) and mutant human tau in double transgenic mice leads to enhanced amyloid deposition and neurofibrillary pathology; and 2) the co-expression leads to neuronal cell death in limbic brain regions.

the crossing of transgenic mice that express human mutant amyloid-beta precursor protein with those expressing human mutant tau resulted in accelerated amyloid deposition and neurofibrillary tangle formation in the brain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
the molecular mechanisms underlying Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative diseases.
the development of a novel class of small molecules, which can selectively target tau protein.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
beta-amyloid is a necessary but not a sufficient factor in the pathogenesis and development of tau alterations.
the Tg2576 mice do not develop tau pathology and that the Tg VLW mice do not develop amyloid deposits.
the amyloid cascade theory is not the only theory, but that it is a very important theory, which should be considered in the development of future therapeutic approaches.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the double mutant APP/TAU mice provide a useful model for studying the complex interplay between amyloid and tau alterations in vivo and for the development of new therapies for Alzheimer's disease.
amyloid-beta deposition and tau pathology are not necessarily causally linked.
the amyloid cascade hypothesis is correct but that tau pathology is not a downstream event of amyloid deposition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
amyloid production/depositon may be the main cause of tau alterations in Alzheimer’s disease.
tau is not just a bystander in AD, it is an active player in the disease process and may be an important therapeutic target.
the interaction between the two major pathologic lesions in Alzheimer's disease may be more complex than initially anticipated.
